data.question: Should we re-adopt block_k 3 (reversing D1), remove sanctions (sanction_lambda 0), adopt only the hold_limit 60 s → 70 s change, or keep v2, given that the two larger gap reductions cost on-time service?
data.background: Options 1 and 3 narrow the main goal, utility_gap, the most (+7.5 and +11.2), but both lower on_time_rate and min_company_on_time_rate, and A voted against both (B also against option 1). Option 1 reverses D1, a decision you adopted against the vote and asked to have re-measured, and it trades C's sanctions against A's blocked time (556 s already), a fairness judgment the on-time gate does not capture. Option 3 narrows the gap by switching off the measurement of road misuse rather than changing road use, so whether that meets 'no company gains or loses because of how the road is used' is a value judgment I should not make for you.

options.summary: block_k 2 → 3 (re-measure of D1). utility_gap improves by +7.5 on 4/5 seeds; utility A / B / C 23.0 / 23.6 / 15.9 (from 25.2 / 25.4 / 10.2). On-time 74.8 (from 80.8), late 7.8 (from 1.8), blocked s 2396 (from 1046), road violations 20.6 (from 26.0), lowest on-time rate 0.83 (from 0.96); on_time_rate 0.91, sanction_total 12.3. Votes A ×, B ×, C ○. Reverses your D1 decision.
options.stakeholders: C gains (fewer sanctions, utility 10.2 → 15.9). A and B lose utility, and A, already absorbing 556 s of blocked time, is likely to absorb more as total blocked time more than doubles. Customers lose: late deliveries rise from 1.8 to 7.8 and the worst company's on-time rate falls to 0.83, which may strain the DELIVERY_SLA.

options.summary: sanction_lambda 0.5 → 0. utility_gap improves by +11.2 on 4/5 seeds; utility A / B / C 23.2 / 27.2 / 25.6. sanction_total 0.0 (from 20.0), but road violations rise to 45.8 (from 26.0), blocked s 1998, on-time 76.0, late 6.6, lowest on-time rate 0.89, on_time_rate 0.92. Votes A ×, B ○, C ○.
options.stakeholders: B and C gain (no sanctions; C 10.2 → 25.6). A loses: it never parks on the road yet keeps absorbing blocked time with no compensation, and its utility falls to 23.2. Customers lose: late deliveries rise from 1.8 to 6.6 and on-time rates drop. The gap narrows mainly because misuse is no longer counted, not because road use became fairer.

options.summary: hold_limit 60 s → 70 s. Passes all gates and can be adopted automatically. utility_gap improves by +1.7 on 4/5 seeds; utility A / B / C 25.0 / 24.7 / 11.5. On-time 80.2, late 2.4, blocked s 1193, road violations 23.6, lowest on-time rate 0.95; on_time_rate 0.97, sanction_total 19.0. Votes A ○, B ×, C ○.
options.stakeholders: C gains slightly (10.2 → 11.5); A and B lose slightly (25.2 → 25.0, 25.4 → 24.7). Customers see a small loss (late 1.8 → 2.4, on_time_rate 0.98 → 0.97, lowest rate 0.96 → 0.95). B voted against it.

options.summary: No change; stay at v2. utility_gap stays as now (utility A / B / C 25.2 / 25.4 / 10.2); on-time 80.8, late 1.8, blocked s 1046, road violations 26.0, lowest on-time rate 0.96, sanction_total 20.0.
options.stakeholders: Customers keep the best measured service. A and B keep their current utility; C stays far behind at 10.2, so the main goal of narrowing the spread is not advanced, which may weaken C's willingness to cooperate.

recommendation.reason: It is the only option that narrows utility_gap (+1.7, 4/5 seeds) without a flagged loss on on_time_rate or min_company_on_time_rate, it keeps D1's intent and the sanction system intact, and it passes the vote. Options 1 and 3 buy larger gap reductions with clearly worse customer service and shift costs onto A (more blocked time, or uncompensated blocked time). If you judge C's lagging utility to be the overriding fairness problem, option 1 or 3 is your call, but I would not choose them on the metric alone.

unknowns: How total blocked time is split between companies under each option; the table gives only totals, and A's 556 s is from the current state.
Why C's utility is low (sanctions from parking vs. demand or routes), and whether C will change its behavior if rules or sanctions change.
Each company's future behavior policy, including whether removing sanctions (option 3) would increase road misuse beyond the measured 45.8 violations over time.
How customers will react to more late deliveries, and whether on-time rates of 0.83–0.92 would breach DELIVERY_SLA commitments.
Actual order volume in the quiet season; the measurements may not reflect the coming period's demand.
Results on the one seed of five that did not improve for each option, and variance with only 5 seeds.
